title: Can algorithms help level the playing field in SME lending? Evidence from Peru
gist: Using a sharp psychometric-score cutoff at a large Peruvian commercial bank's 2012-13 SME lending pilot, researchers show that gender gaps in credit run through loan officer discretion, not outright rejection: below the cutoff women were 18 percentage points less likely to take a loan and got loans about 60 percent smaller, while above the cutoff — where approval was fully automated — the gaps vanished with no rise in default rates. The key design feature was that the algorithm used alternative psychometric data rather than historical approval decisions that would have encoded past bias.

themes.theme: Where the SME gender credit gap actually originates

insights.claim: Women entrepreneurs whose firms are virtually identical to men's in size, sector and performance are still less likely to receive a loan and tend to receive smaller amounts on worse terms.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: An unpriced creditworthy borrower pool is an arbitrage for lenders willing to underwrite it — the gap is a mispricing, not a risk premium.
insights.quote: Women entrepreneurs across the world are creditworthy. They are just not always treated that way.
insights.locator: Women entrepreneurs across the world are creditworthy

insights.claim: Loan officers rely on soft information from interviews, site visits and personal impressions, and that discretion opens the door to biased judgments especially where officers have limited experience lending to SMEs or to women.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Bias concentrates in inexperienced lending desks, so portfolio-level gender gaps are a diagnostic for underdeveloped SME underwriting capability.
insights.locator: Loan officers often rely on “soft information”

insights.claim: Below the psychometric cutoff, where loan officers decided, women and men were equally likely to receive a loan offer, but women were 18 percentage points less likely to take out a loan and received loans about 60 percent smaller than comparable male applicants.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Approval-rate parity masks a 60% size gap — headline approval statistics are the wrong metric for measuring lending discrimination.
insights.quote: women are 18 percentage points less likely to take out a loan and receive loans that are about 60 percent smaller than those offered to comparable male applicants
insights.locator: First, when loan officers play a central role

insights.claim: Gender bias in SME lending operates mainly through loan terms rather than outright rejection.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Regulators and lenders auditing only for denial disparities will find nothing; terms-level auditing is where the signal lives.
insights.quote: This suggests bias operates mainly through loan terms, not outright rejection.
insights.locator: First, when loan officers play a central role

insights.claim: The study used a 2012-13 SME lending pilot at one of Peru's largest commercial banks, which had a small SME portfolio at the time and was experimenting with ways to scale up lending.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The setting is a bank building SME capability from a low base — the closest analog to fintech lenders entering underbanked segments today.
insights.locator: To answer this question, we partnered with one of Peru's largest commercial banks

insights.claim: Applicants completed a psychometric assessment from the Entrepreneurial Finance Lab that generated a credit score from traits such as problem-solving ability, integrity and personality, without using past loan approvals.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Psychometric scoring is a live alternative-data underwriting channel for thin-file borrowers, validated here against two years of default data.
insights.locator: As part of the pilot, applicants completed a psychometric assessment

insights.claim: A sharp score cutoff automatically offered a loan with size mechanically tied to the score above it, while applicants below went through the traditional discretionary loan officer process, creating a clean regression discontinuity.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The design isolates discretion itself as the treatment, making this rare causal rather than correlational evidence on algorithmic lending.
insights.quote: Because borrowers just above and just below the cutoff are otherwise very similar, this setup allows us to isolate how outcomes change when loan officer discretion is removed.
insights.locator: The key feature of the pilot was a sharp cutoff score

themes.theme: Automation eliminated the gap without raising risk

insights.claim: Above the automatic-approval cutoff, where decisions were fully automated, there were no differences between women and men in loan approval, take-up or loan size.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Complete gap elimination from a single design change means the constraint was institutional process, not borrower demand or capability.
insights.quote: these gender gaps disappear entirely under automatic approval
insights.locator: Second, these gender gaps disappear entirely

insights.claim: Tracking borrowers for up to two years showed no increase in default rates for automatically approved loans for either gender, with women displaying slightly lower default rates overall.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Removes the standard objection that inclusive lending buys volume with credit quality — the equity gain here was free.
insights.quote: If anything, women display slightly lower default rates overall.
insights.locator: Third, eliminating discretion does not come at the cost

insights.claim: Loan take-up rose sharply within six months of application for women exactly at the automatic approval cutoff while men's take-up changed little.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The discontinuity is female-specific, confirming the binding constraint was applied selectively rather than being a general credit-supply effect.
insights.quote: The figure shows a sharp increase in loan take‑up within six months of the loan application for women exactly at the automatic approval cutoff, while men’s loan take‑up changes little.

themes.theme: Algorithm design is what determines fairness

insights.claim: Algorithms do not automatically eliminate bias, and systems trained on historical lending data can replicate or even reinforce existing discrimination.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The result is not a blanket endorsement of automated underwriting — training-data provenance is the variable that determines outcomes and regulatory exposure.
insights.quote: Algorithms do not automatically eliminate bias.

insights.claim: The Peruvian system was gender-neutral because the psychometric tool used alternative data rather than past approval decisions that already embed bias, combined with restricted officer discretion.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Two-part recipe — alternative data plus discretion limits — is the actionable design spec for lenders building inclusive underwriting models.
insights.quote: By restricting discretion while avoiding biased training data, the automated system turned out to be more gender‑neutral than human judgment.

insights.claim: Equity and efficiency can go together in credit markets, since eliminating gender bias in this case neither increased default risk nor weakened portfolio performance.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Undercuts the trade-off framing used to resist inclusion mandates, strengthening the case for supervisory pressure on lending-terms disparities.
insights.locator: Equity and efficiency can go together

insights.claim: As digital lending spreads across developing economies the relevant question is no longer whether algorithms will shape credit markets but how they are designed and governed.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Signals that model governance and data-provenance rules are the next regulatory frontier for emerging-market digital lenders.
insights.quote: the question is no longer whether algorithms will shape credit markets, but how they are designed and governed
insights.locator: As digital lending tools spread across developing economies

insights.claim: Differences in credit access between men and women constrain both firm performance and broader economic development because SMEs are a key engine of job creation and growth.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Frames the lending gap as an aggregate growth drag, which is the argument that moves it from a CSR item to a central-bank and finance-ministry concern.
